#3126. Zane Lowe shares Apple Music Radio audience numbers, recalls ‘crickets’ in the early days

In a new interview with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, Apple Music’s Zane Lowe discussed the early days of Apple Music Radio and revealed just how many people tune in each month. Here are the details.

Apple is rarely terribly specific about how many people use its services, including how many tune in to its radio stations.

In 2019, for instance, Eddy Cue said Beats 1 (now Apple Music 1) had ‘tens of millions of listeners,’ but Apple has rarely provided more specific figures since.

Apple Music’s Zane Lowe, however, has now offered a more concrete figure, revealing that the service reaches over 50 million unique listeners every month:

We were never, you know, delusional enough to assume we were going to get a huge audience overnight. We’d have to build it like anyone else would have to build anything. But we’ve just got to a point in our 11 years on where we now, overall, reach over 50 million unique listeners a month, which is a really large number for us, and it’s growing exponentially and really fast.

The revelation came in a wide-ranging interview published today with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, where Lowe discussed Apple Music Radio’s early struggles, its approach to supporting emerging artists, and why human curation remains central to the service.

When discussing the early days at Apple Music, Lowe recalled:

When we started the radio here, I didn’t have access or opportunity with a lot of the artists that I built relationships with from the BBC because we were unproven. And I came over here thinking, “Well, I’ve got Jimmy Iovine over here, and I’ve got Apple over here and I feel unstoppable, and who’s not going to want to come and launch this thing with us?” But it was kind of crickets… As upsetting as that was at the time, two good things came out of it. Number one, it snapped me back into the reality force field of building something from scratch. And number two, it made us focus really clearly and in a big way on new and emerging artists.

He also mentioned some of the first artists Apple Music Radio supported, including Billie Eilish with “Ocean Eyes,” Khalid with American Teen, and Bryson Tiller with his first song.

At the time, Lowe noted, these artists were just getting started, and supporting emerging talent became a defining part of Apple Music Radio’s approach, one that continues to this day:

The really cool number is on our radio network. We played — this year alone — over 6,500 individual artists, which is not a commercial radio model. [Other radio networks’] playlists are very small, and the amount of plays is very great. Our playlist is gigantic. We play a lot of different artists, and over half of those 6,500 artists we’ve played in one year are new or emerging. So, think about 3,300 artists, roughly, getting played, who may be on their first song, their first EP, their first album…It’s proof of concept. It’s great.

Still on the subject of the early days at Apple Music, Lowe said “it was very clear [from the start] that that was very important to everybody who was responsible for bringing Apple Music to life,” adding that “serving artists and the artistic community in a way that is of most value and of most service” still drives “a lot of the decision-making” at the platform.

When the conversation turned to Apple Music’s recent rebranding, which introduced a new logo physically created using sound waves from a composition by Fred again.., Lowe said he couldn’t speak to the decisions behind it, but stressed the human element and the creative process that went into it:

We could have created that in a way that could utilize all of the tech available. We could type that into a prompt. But at the end of the day, seeing how it’s made is so much more additionally inspiring than just seeing it. It speaks to, I think, what we try to do here, which is, we love the process of what we do, and the result is a byproduct of getting to do it and loving to do it.

The issue of algorithms also came up when Lowe discussed Apple Music’s approach to music discovery, with the executive emphasizing the importance of human curation over automated recommendations:

Well, we don’t want to say that too loudly, because someone could be like, “Wait a minute, we could cut costs here? Man, how did we not think of that!” Look, I mean, jokes aside, we’ve been incredibly fortunate, and I’ve been incredibly fortunate to take that step from the BBC into a company and to work with people that value exactly what it is you’re describing: this idea of place and this experience of sharing things with each other, and how meaningful it is when someone shares a record with you and it comes with context. It’s a gift…

#3125. I Didn’t Expect to Like Xiaomi’s Bizarre Dual-Screen Phone So Much

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Review: Xiaomi's 18 Pro Max is a quirky Android phone that stands out from the crowd with its extra screen on the back. Shame Americans can't have it.

Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe

Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe

Xiaomi teased me with the 17 Pro, its bizarre dual-screen Android phone, last year. But it was sold only in China. Being from the UK, I went back to my regular boring phone with its boring single screen. Big sigh. So imagine my excitement when Xiaomi announced that its new flagship 18 Pro and Pro Max — complete with a second rear screen — would launch internationally, with a rollout including the UK and wider Europe. As with the rest of Xiaomi’s handsets, people in the US are flat out of luck.

That sucks for Americans because this phone is actually damn good. I worried that the rear screen would just be a dumb gimmick — something that tries to separate the phone from competitors but doesn’t actually add anything useful. But I actually like it. Need it? No. But it’s fun and has some genuine uses.

Beyond the screen, though, the 18 Pro Max packs the latest Qualcomm Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor, a fast-charging silicon-carbon battery and a potent camera setup that utilizes the same LOFIC sensor technology that impressed me so much in Xiaomi and Leica’s Leitzphone earlier this year.

The 18 Pro isn’t just smaller (6.4 inches vs. the Pro Max’s 6.9 inches) it misses some of the Max’s top tech as well. The processor is a lesser model, the main camera doesn’t use LOFIC tech and the smaller battery isn’t as capable. Shame.

But the 18 Pro Max is an all-round Android powerhouse, and I’ve really enjoyed getting to grips with it over the past couple of weeks. Here’s what I’ve found and what you need to know about this phone.

The extra display on the back is certainly this phone’s standout feature. It’s basically in the same place as the iPhone 18 Pro’s camera island, but instead of just being a piece of metal, it’s an actual functioning screen. If you’ve ever seen the cover display on a clamshell flip phone like Samsung’s Galaxy Z Flip 8, then it’ll seem quite familiar.

Like the Flip 8, the second display shows incoming notifications, acting as a camera viewfinder and offering a variety of basic built-in functions like calendar reminders. What really hooked me, though, was the ability to create Gen AI apps just by typing in a prompt.

For example, I asked for “a game where you just pop bubbles,” which the “Polish” tool elaborated on with deeper functions and visual styles before generating a finished game that was fully playable on the back screen, complete with a scoring system and, for some reason, a jellyfish mascot. It takes about 5 minutes for the app to be created each time, and its functions are limited. It’s not able to access any app data, so don’t expect to create a new email reader, and anything too technical will result in failure.

I asked it to create a camera overlay that showed exposure settings (shutter speed, ISO and so on) to serve as a light meter for an analog camera. I’m not sure whether the issue was my explanation or a technical limitation, but it took the phone two tries to get something close. It created an interface with dials and exposure information, but it didn’t open the camera to calculate exposure as I’d hoped. As a result, it looked nice but it was functionally redundant.

Another time, I asked it to create an app that showed real-time charging speeds. The resulting app showed current battery level but not charging speed. It did have a baffling “charging milestones completed” button that simply increased by one each time I tapped it. I also had no luck with my “rude word generator,” which just repeatedly came back with “Couldn’t generate.” Frustratingly, each time it fails to create an app, it doesn’t tell you why — like if you’re asking for information it’s unable to access — but just says to try again “in a minute or two,” which rarely resulted in success in my testing time. If I’m asking for something it can’t achieve, it’d be helpful to know that.

Even so, I’m impressed with this app creation tool and, like many of the AI tools that only mildly excite me right now, I can only assume it will improve over time.

One of my favorite uses of the rear screen, though, is for vlogging. Firstly, seeing yourself from the back of the phone means you’re able to accurately film yourself using the best quality camera, rather than limiting yourself to the front-facing camera, which won’t look as good. But there’s also an autocue function where you can input a script and have it overlaid as text, allowing you to read out your words as you present to camera.

It’s a powerful tool for vloggers and other video creators who rely on longer prewritten scripts for their videos. But it’s quite basic: the text simply auto-scrolls at a speed you set in advance. I’d love to see Xiaomi use voice recognition here to automatically progress the text as you read out the words, slowing down or speeding up as you naturally read aloud. This tech already exists, so I don’t think I’m asking for literal magic here.

Tucked into that second display is a 200-megapixel main camera and a 200-megapixel telephoto camera offering 3.2x optical zoom or 6.4x hybrid zoom. There’s also a really tiny 50-megapixel ultrawide camera by itself below the camera island, which makes it feel like an afterthought — something that I’ll come back to later.

The main sensor is physically slightly smaller than the one in Xiaomi’s Leitzphone, but it uses the same LOFIC sensor tech for better dynamic range in a single image. I’ve taken a lot of photos with it so far and I’m really impressed with what I’ve seen. The smaller 18 Pro has an almost identical camera setup but its main sensor doesn’t use LOFIC, which is a shame as it forces you to go for the larger phone if you want the best possible image quality.

Shots are well-exposed, with accurate colors and fine details that manage to look sharp but without the harsh over-sharpened look that’s all too often seen from phone cameras. Images look more natural as a result.

There are a lot of ways to tune your images in-camera — almost too many, in fact. There’s a whole host of built-in color presets, including a Leica-branded high-contrast black-and-white mode that I like, all of which you can customize further by adjusting the tones, colors, grain and white balance. Then there’s the option to shoot using the phone’s default color processing, going with “Leica Vibrant” for more popping colors or “Leica Authentic” for more natural tones. Each of these applies no matter what filter you then apply over the top.

Confused? Yeah, I’m not entirely surprised, there are a lot of variables at play when taking an image with this thing but it didn’t take me long to figure out how to get the look that I wanted. And let’s be honest, there aren’t many photographers who want fewer options in how to take a photo.

Then there’s Essential Moment, which is its own standalone mode where you can select from three distinct styles: a black and white mode, “modern vintage,” or “Iconic CCD.” Each of these is designed to replicate specific looks from cameras of the past, and Xiaomi says it uses AI to analyze the scene to authentically reproduce color tones, vintage lens effects and film grain (though crucially not generative AI to actually alter anything in the scene).

I actually love this, especially the black and white option, which produces monochrome images with beautiful contrast and genuinely authentic-looking film grain. It’s the mode I’d end up using most often, I’m sure, and I’ve taken a bunch of photos with it that I really like.

Oh, and that tiny ultrawide camera, weirdly separated from its friends? It’s not great, with nighttime shots being particularly disappointing here. On the upside, the main camera’s standard focal length is 23mm, which is already pretty wide, so you probably won’t miss the ultrawide much.

While the base 18 Pro uses Qualcomm’s latest Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6, the Pro Max ups the ante with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. It’s no surprise that the Pro Max is a seriously powerful bit of kit, returning benchmark scores up there with the powerhouse Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra. Everything ran exceptionally smoothly, from playing demanding 3D games like Genshin Impact to editing photos or navigating the Android 17 interface. I found much the same with the 18 Pro, too — I didn’t see a noticeable difference in performance.

I don’t mind Xiaomi’s software skin, as it’s easy enough for anyone familiar with Android to get to grips with. What I don’t like, though, is the company’s insistence on preloading it with an armada of apps including AliExpress, Netflix, WPS Office, TikTok and others. Together with the variety of Xiaomi apps also on board, the phone feels somewhat cluttered before you’ve even had a chance to add anything of your own. I’ve seen worse examples (Oppo has been bad with this), but it still irks me that the phone ends up feeling almost like it’s ad-supported. And if it is, surely it should be cheaper?

It helps a bit, sure, but it won’t block those creeps entirely. My advice is: if you’ve got information so sensitive that even a glimpse would be career-ending, maybe wait until you’re alone before you put it on screen.

The 7,050-mAh silicon-carbon battery in the larger Pro Max packs a punch, putting in some solid scores on our demanding battery rundown tests. After one hour of YouTube streaming, it dropped to 97%, then to 89% after the third hour. That puts it above the Galaxy S26 Ultra and Google Pixel 11 Pro XL, although still below the current champion, the iPhone 18 Pro Max.

In everyday use, you won’t struggle to get through a full day of mixed use and you can likely be quite demanding with it and still not worry about it conking out mid-afternoon. Take photos, watch videos, listen to music – don’t stress over it; this thing should hold out fine.

The phone supports up to 100-watt wired fast charging, though you’ll need a Xiaomi fast charger to achieve the fastest speeds. I don’t have a Xiaomi charger (and the fastest it sells in the UK is 90W for £25), but I tried it with multiple third-party 100-watt chargers and the maximum I could get was around 65 watts. Even so, it went from 1% to 65% in 30 minutes of charging, which is still pretty quick — on par with the iPhone 18 Pro Max, in fact. Still, it should be able to go faster; you’ll just need to source a charger that will allow it.

With its smaller 6,000-mAh battery the Xiaomi 18 Pro didn’t fare as well on our battery drain tests (it dropped to 93% after an hour of YouTube streaming) but in general use you’ll still comfortably get through most of a day on a single charge.

If you’re in the US, it’s something of a moot point. You can’t buy it. Sorry. Sure, you can probably import it from some third-party resellers, but it’s not officially on sale.

If you’re somewhere where you can buy it, then lucky you — this phone is a blast. It ticks many of the boxes I’d expect from a flagship phone right now (camera quality in particular), and that second rear screen is the cherry on top. I expected it to feel like a pointless gimmick, and maybe it is a bit of a novelty, but it’s fun and I’ve already found it genuinely useful.

I don’t like that there are so many hardware differences between the two phone sizes, as it forces you to have a much bigger model if you want the best performance. I prefer Apple’s approach: With the iPhone 18 Pro, I can have the same exact potent camera setup and processor performance, no matter which size I choose. With Xiaomi’s phones I’m forced to compromise between performance and pocketability. If you want the best camera, then go for the bigger model. Battery life is better, too.

#3124. Lost or stolen Windows laptop? IT can lock it down without wiping it now

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Windows > Windows 11

The Intune-enabled feature will allow admins to remotely lock down any compromised Windows device.

Microsoft is testing a new feature that lets IT admins instantly lock down your lost or stolen device via remote connection, protecting your work projects and personal data from theft and unauthorized access.

Also: Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now

The new remote lock feature is designed to work in tandem with other Microsoft services, such as Intune and BitLocker, to manage a fleet of devices both in-office and remotely across the globe.

Once a device is reported missing or stolen, an admin can disable login access from anywhere without having to fully wipe the laptop or smartphone. Microsoft reports that the lockdown will persist across restarts, even if the device is disconnected from Wi-Fi networks, and can only be lifted by an admin. This means that thieves can’t use your passwords, PINs, or biometric data to circumvent the lock.

While the new feature allows IT admins to respond quickly when a laptop or phone is reported missing, there are still security gaps that other Windows controls must address. The new lock feature doesn’t erase your data or wipe your device if it can’t be recovered, nor does it isolate the missing device from corporate networks. Therefore, IT admins will still need to access those controls via the Intune and Microsoft Entra dashboards.

Also: You can now restore Windows 11 even if it can’t boot up

The remote lock feature also doesn’t change your Microsoft account credentials, so you can use your log-ins on other devices to recover your data, change passwords, and temporarily disable permissions. Finally, Remote lock doesn’t block the device from being booted in Safe Mode, from a USB, in Windows Recovery Mode, or if the storage drive is reimaged; Microsoft highly recommends keeping BitLocker enabled until the device can be wiped or recovered.

Setting up the remote lock is a straightforward process: Log into the Intune management center, then go to Devices > Windows > Configuration > Create > New Policy > Windows 10 and later > Templates > Custom. This lets admins create a profile for each network-connected device and a device group reserved for lockdown. Locking down a device is as simple as adding it to the group. To unlock, create a second profile and device group, and move the locked device to the new unlock category.

#3122. Microsoft blames major outage on a July update defect – and two other factors

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

A surprise defect took more than 80% of Microsoft's servers out at the outage's peak. Here's what happened.

Microsoft has released new information explaining the massive outage that started Thursday morning and affected Microsoft 365, Copilot, and Outlook access in 74 countries, according to Downdetector.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform, posted early Monday morning that the outage was due to three factors, including a “latent defect” from a July update to Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers. Low server capacity and peak traffic in the US brought the defect out of hiding, despite no prior reported issues.

“A latent defect caused servers to become overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions. This was due to lock contention inside an internal process which caused the machine to become unavailable,” Lamanna said, noting that the update was deployed safely worldwide without any issues for over three months.

He said Microsoft didn’t find the issue in testing due to “the different traffic and SKU mix used in our test labs,” because “our load testing tended to focus on our weaker hardware SKUs with fewer cores.”

Also: Microsoft fixes over 1,000 Windows flaws – and one is being exploited

Two other factors made matters worse, and left servers useless in less than two hours.

“A surge in load increased the likelihood for the networking gateways to encounter the contention,” Lamanna said, explaining that Microsoft 365 maintains two gateway systems. Before the outage started, Teams failed from one to the other, which “changed its traffic patterns.” Simultaneously, he added, “nearly 14% of server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service due to an unrelated issue from the previous day.”

Those two conditions collided and “caused the network gateway to encounter the latent bug from July,” Lamanna concluded. Requests eventually overloaded servers, at which point they stopped responding. At the outage’s low point, over 80% of its servers weren’t responding.

“When servers lose connectivity, our traffic management systems automatically route users to other healthy endpoints,” Lamanna said. “However, the redirected traffic increased the likelihood for the same problem to occur on the remaining endpoints. This caused a cascading failure from server to server as the same amount of load was spread across fewer servers.”

Also: AI finds zero-day flaws for just $4 now – even mediocre hackers can cash in

Before Microsoft issued an explanation, some suspected the outage may have been the result of a cyberattack, which both Lamanna and Microsoft’s status account denied.

It’s unclear how many people the outage affected, though Microsoft’s own numbers from January say Microsoft 365 “exceeds 450 million commercial paid seats,” illustrating the scale of the issue. Microsoft deployed an update to fix the outage and gradually applied it to groups of servers. Lamanna said Microsoft would publish a full post-incident review with more details later this week.

Service might be restored, but customers aren’t happy about having lost nearly two full workdays. One think tank told CNN it estimated the outage — which lasted through close of business on Friday for some — resulted in $7 billion in losses, due to many businesses and organizations being unable to access their everyday systems.

Also: If the November Windows update fails to install on your PC, here’s what to do

The fact that Microsoft’s testing couldn’t find the July issue ahead of time may leave customers wondering when the next dormant defect will strike, and whether the company is prepared.

Organizations across Europe have been leaving Microsoft in recent years, opting instead for locally-controlled, open-source alternatives. The former CEO of Github launched a decentralized alternative called Entire earlier this year, citing developers’ need for something more reliable, as Github has similarly been plagued with outages.

For many, Teams was barely offline over the two-day period, or was the first service to come back online.

“Several services like Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint, and Office apps failed out of the faulty network gateway infrastructure. That is why those services were restored earlier, with Teams chats and meetings functioning without issue for most of the outage,” Lamanna explained. Other services like Exchange Online can’t fail out.

He added that fixing the outage was slow because waiting traffic hit servers as soon as they came back, rendering them unresponsive just as quickly.

“Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state,” Lamanna said. “Additionally, since the main code defect was a latent bug from several months previous, our normal rollback, flighting, and feature flags were unable to quickly revert the change.”

On Thursday morning, people began reporting issues with Outlook, Teams, and Copilot, according to Downdetector. By 1 p.m. ET, the number of reported Outlook outages was nearly 83,000 but had fallen to just under 75,000 by 2:38 p.m. ET. Teams and Copilot reports started dropping significantly by Thursday evening, but many individuals were still reporting issues accessing systems well into Friday morning on X and Reddit. Even Microsoft’s status page was down until around 3 p.m. ET Thursday.

Also: If the November Windows update fails to install on your PC, here’s what to do

As late as Friday afternoon, the company didn’t yet have an ETA of when the outage would be fully solved.

We draw against this $1 million over time against 70% of our acquisition spend each month.

After the principal's repaid is when that premium is actually paid. What that premium is, if we look at the next slide, it depends on the speed of the payback. You can see here on the right side, the different ranges of payback speeds, and if you fall within those ranges, you can see the percentages there.

Once the principal plus the premium has been paid for a cohort, General Catalyst's participation in that particular cohort ends, at which point then all the profit from those cohorts is ours, and it had been pre-funded in a strong cash flow sort of way. This structure allows us to fund the portion of acquisition investment with the future receipts each cohort's intended to generate. Also a reminder, this financing is non-dilutive. There are going to be a lot of end cards available at the offline retailers. We're going to be also driving a lot of online to offline traffic, which we haven't done before. I think the great thing is that, again, with Care Bears and the hydration products, these are already, I would say, at least in the wellness supplement category, two of the most sought-after products that people search in retail.

Then, again, going back to all of the brand investment that we're making now, when we are in retail, people will recognize IM8 already. Because the last thing you want, and a lot of the reasons, again, I study a lot of this stuff in terms of go-to-market strategy, is when a brand gets into retail and there's no demand. You need to be able to drive that demand because no one recognizes that brand. I think a lot of the brand equity, the brand investments that we're making today are going to pay off significantly when we get into retail channel.

Susan Anderson: Yeah. Okay, great. Then maybe just one follow-up. I was curious just kind of the-

Danny Yeung: Also, Susan Anderson, one other thing I can add that's also going to be a big plus for us, for Care Bears specifically, is that next year is Care Bears' 45th anniversary. So by default, Care Bears by themselves are going to be doing lots of offline physical activations, online as well. So that's naturally going to help us in terms of brand recognition or people understanding the brand better.

Susan Anderson: Yeah. Okay, great. Thanks so much.

Operator: Thank you, Susan. Our next question will be from Jonna Kim of TD Cowen. Jonah? Jonah, please unmute.

Jonna Kim: All right. Thank you for taking my question. Hi, Danny. Hi, Brian. On IM8 itself, how do you think about the distribution opportunity going forward? Is there room to expand in the retail? Is your strategy different as you look towards next year? Thank you.

Danny Yeung: Yeah. As mentioned now, we definitely plan to go into retail. Again, I think even from an investor perspective, this makes the business much more investable because we're not just a direct-to-consumer brand. People will be able to see us on the shelves. As mentioned, by 2027, we will have at least a hydration and Care Bears brand inside retail. So 100% on retail. In terms of our ambassador relationships, we look at a lot of our ambassador relationships on a case-by-case basis. As I mentioned earlier, every single one of these big ambassadors that comes in, they found us.

Normally, it's through a recommendation by their nutritionist, their doctor, or a friend, and they're taking the product, they're enjoying the product, they're using the product daily, and they come find us. I think these are the best type of partnerships where these ambassadors, they start off as users first, and they come in, and they want to partner with us. A lot of people ask me, Who are we going to sign up next? The reality is, I don't know who's going to reach out to us next, right? Once they reach out, we see if it's a fit for the brand.

Of course, it also has to fit in terms of the commercials, but because these individuals love IM8 so much, we're always able to get really good partnerships out of these.

Jonna Kim: Just one last question on, obviously, New Year is an important period for wellness products, and you're at a larger scale. Is there anything you are doing different in terms of your marketing strategy around the New Year time?

Danny Yeung: Yeah, I would say Q4 and Q1, right? I mean, Q4 and Q1 are going to be the biggest seasonality aspects in the business-wise. From Q1, again, new year, new you, so we will be launching hydration products in Q1, so I think that's going to be different, along with our current Essentials and Longevity products. One key thing I think you're going to see us continue to do is that we're continuing to do a lot of offline activation events, and you'll continue to see that, especially when we launch Hydration, because naturally, there's going to be many multiple flavors.

Our offline events, again, since 22 months ago, and that's one thing that really separates us from everyone else, is that people can see the product, they can talk to our scientific advisory board, they can talk to our ambassadors. I meet with them. So we've done now 200 plus events in the last 22 months, and I think that really puts a face to the product as well. I think with Hydration, we're going to do more of these type of activation events around the world.

Jonna Kim: No, thank you for the follow-up.

Operator: Thank you, Jonna. We'll go next to Alex Nowak of Lucid. Alex, you may proceed.

Alex Nowak: Okay, great. Good morning, everyone. Thanks for taking the time. Appreciate it. We talked a lot about the CAC throughout the call, but I just really want to keep it simple. Again, I think Hydration we believe is a big category. Care Bears is a big category.

But we're so focused on growing the business today with new product development, growing existing business. We just felt at 400, it gives a lot of investors upside opportunities for us to capture on that.

Alex Nowak: Yep, absolutely. Even your shareholder letter mentioned, the plan behind 2027 sums to more than $400 million, so totally get that. I do want to go back on our prior point about partners, and you've added some really good partners. Any particular sports that you would-

Danny Yeung: So we are looking to a few different individuals that can really help us push the envelope in China for when we launch in 2027. Besides that, again, every day it's been crazy busy, right? I think we're very excited and happy with our existing roster. So, I can't tell you that there's a specific new area that we're looking to from an ambassador partnership perspective. Like you said, Alex, I mean, the running club piece is a huge opportunity for Hydration, right? I think around the world you see running clubs being developed. Regardless if it's 50 people, 100 people. Diplo's running club is now 10,000 people, and he only started this like a year ago.

So that's a prime opportunity to be able to promote our Hydration product when it comes out in Q1.

Alex Nowak: Absolutely. All right. Well, thank you for the time. Appreciate it.

Operator: Thank you, Alex. Our next question comes from Ryan Meyers of Lake Street. Ryan?

Ryan Meyers: Hey, guys. Thanks for taking my questions. First one for me, just on the topic of the General Catalyst financing. With the financing now operating for a full quarter, how should we think about the relationship between new funding and repayments as the facility matures? Then maybe at what point do you think the business can begin generating positive operating cash flow independent of the General Catalyst funding?

Brian Rosin: Yeah, I mean, in the quarter, we repaid $7 million against draws of $31 million, then they owed us a few million at the end of the quarter as well. For quite some time, the amount that we're going to be drawing down for each individual month is going to exceed any of the repayment amounts in aggregate for a good amount of time. As you look out and you model the business into the future, it's more like, I would say 18 months into the arrangement is when I start to see the cash coming in more or less equivalent to the cash being repaid to them. So at that point, it becomes cash neutral.

However, cash neutral is a much different environment than us funding our own acquisition dollars at that point in time. Depending on how large the business is at that point and how much we're spending per month, that would all be our own cash out the door, whereas in this world, cash neutral in that environment is still really strong from a cash flow standpoint. You asked about when we would potentially be turning operating cash flow positive. It's similar to when we would potentially turn adjusted EBITDA positive, and we've not wanted to get too far ahead of ourselves in trying to guide when specifically that will happen.

That will, again, we don't want to put any specific timelines on it, but I would say it's not that far out into the future when that would happen, and it all comes down to how much are we able to keep spending at our 3-to-1 return at near our $300-ish CAC. We've been able to keep spending more and more at that number, and as time goes on, if we can continue to do that, then that'll just keep pushing out that chasm. But if we slow the growth or if we slow the spend, that number would come very fast.

We could become profitable next quarter if we slowed our spend, but that's not in the best interest of our shareholders long term.

Ryan Meyers: Okay, got it. Secondly, maybe for Danny Yeung, can you just sort of provide us with some commentary on what you think is allowing the IM8 brand specifically to drive the above average customer retention when it comes to supplements?

Danny Yeung: It is quite simple actually, right, on that part, because the product works. I think, again, starting from day one-wise, right, we had an amazing scientific advisory board, third-party testing, NSF certification. Then so when you drink it over a long period of time, you form a routine, it works, and you will continue with it. Then so I think that is the main reason why I think retention has been so powerful, right? I think we have also really focused not just on the functionality of it, but at the same time also on the taste. When we just launched, we had one flavor. We have now introduced two new flavors.

In Q1, we are going to introduce another flavor. So I think having these new updates on the formulation as well as on taste continually delights our existing customer base.

Ryan Meyers: Makes sense. Thanks for taking my questions.

Operator: Thank you, Ryan. We will go next to Tom Forte of Maxim. Tom?

Tom Forte: Great. Thanks, Shannon. Danny and Brian, thanks for taking my questions. I have two on artificial intelligence, and I am going to ask them at the same time. Can you give an update on how you are able to leverage artificial intelligence to scale the business without adding material headcount? Second, on agentic commerce, Meta has had tremendous engagement based on the number of downloads for Muse. How are you positioning yourselves to capitalize on that opportunity?

Danny Yeung: Great question, Tom. Good to connect. I think on the first part, in terms of how we're using AI, I think, again, if you look at least the direct-to-consumer space, the key thing actually for any company in this space is content. You need to have lots of content across many different channels. A lot of the aspects that we do use is basically utilizing AI to develop lots of content, regardless if it's static videos in combination with real shot videos and basically utilizing AI to cut them through to much more different content pieces.

So, for example, one of the clear examples, I think I shared this previously, is that if you look at our Meta public ads library, at any given time, we'll have three, four, 5,000 ads running live at any given time. What we'll do, we'll be able to utilize AI to identify the winners very fast. When we do identify winners, we'll then show these same ads on AppLovin, on X, on Snap, on TikTok, the same aspects. On a weekly basis, we're also testing a lot of new content, five, six, 700 pieces of content on a weekly basis, which, again, to be fair, if you don't know what you're doing, it's very, very difficult.

That's why there are very few brands that can scale at our levels. I think that gives you a clear example. That's why, again, even right now, if you look at our overall team base, we have approximately 70, 75 employees. If you think about our full-year revenue this year, which is going to be well more than $200 million, so it's roughly about $3 million revenue per employee per year. If we think about next year, looking at $400 million plus, we'll probably add 25, 30 people, so probably get to about 100 employees at $400 million. So that would be roughly about $4 million per employee per year. So we believe which are great metrics, right?

In terms of the agentic commerce piece, great question. Right now, we're actually testing in terms of even having ads within ChatGPT, which they've already opened up. I do believe it's still early days, but it's going to move very, very fast, right? I do believe within the next three to six months, or even a shorter pair of times, a lot of people are going to be using their AI to purchase things. Even for me, I'm using Muse, Instinct to buy things with that AI. So I couldn't imagine that's going to be a common place in the next three, six, 12 months.

Again, given the amount of work that we're already in this, we're doing with AI, we feel that we'll be able to lead the pack in that area.

Operator: Our next question will come from Dylan Hines of B. Riley. Dylan, please go ahead.

Dylan Hines: Hey, great quarter. Thanks for taking the question. I just wanted to go back to the retail entry. Do you already have agreements with retail partners, and could you maybe provide any color on that, maybe which ones? Then what would the ramp look like? When do you expect, you think, you'll include the retail launch into guidance?

Danny Yeung: Yeah, so I think in terms of the retail aspect, transparently, we do not have any agreements. We've been, again, we've been hounded by all the major retail partners, I would say, for the last 12 months. This is something that I'm personally involved with in terms of working closely with that big box retailer. Again, we can't mention the name, but it's a big name in the US retail space, right? We expect that to go live by the end of 2027. I do believe right now it's still way too early to provide any type of guidance in terms of what that is.

Again, for us-wise, we're very optimistic about the opportunity given this big box retailer and our product scope and our product set that we have in place. Once we are in retail, I think very soon we will be able to give guidance in terms of how big the opportunity is.

Dylan Hines: Okay, got you. Going to the ambassador network, do you have any specific plans in terms of activations with the ambassadors? How do you convert the following visibility and subscriptions? Can you try to quantify any of the benefit from the ambassadors?

Danny Yeung: Yeah, 100%. I think every single one of our ambassadors have more than paid much more than what we have given them. It is actually quite easy for us to quantify. It is not just from the. To be fair, the offline activations is more brand activity events. For example, when we have a partnership with Giannis, Aryna Sabalenka, et cetera, one of the key things for us is content and digital profiling. We are able to utilize partnership and white listing ads. For example, Giannis, he has 20 million followers on Instagram. So we can market from Giannis's handle or Aryna's handle to their followers.

Speaker 4: From morning fields to star aisles, every fruit and vegetable is handpicked with care, sorted and checked at our collection centers, packed fresh and sent straight away, so farm freshness reaches star and your plate.

Dylan Hines: Gotcha. Okay, great. Thanks for taking the question.

Operator: Thank you, Dylan Hines. Our next question comes from George Kelly of Roth. George, please go ahead.

George Kelly: Everybody, thanks. Can you hear me?

George Kelly: Hey, Danny Yeung. Thanks for taking the questions. A couple for you. I will start with, I think I heard in the prepared remarks that you are changing manufacturing partners. And of course, for the gummies, that is going to be a separate manufacturer as well.

George Kelly: I guess for the core product, though, are there changes coming?

Danny Yeung: For the core product, we're adding additional capacity, just in case. Because right now, to be fair, our scale is where we can't just be dependent on one manufacturer. So we're also adding another manufacturer just in case anything happens, right?

George Kelly: Okay. Understood. Second question from me, back to your guidance revision, the EBITDA change. Is it fair to say that I guess I'm just trying to dig into the trends you've seen with respect to CAC in October and November, and I'm wondering if there's been something that maybe wasn't fully appreciated in your prior guide. Maybe it's the election. Just trying to understand how CAC has changed versus your earlier expectations.

Danny Yeung: I mean, it hasn't changed much on a quarter-to-quarter basis, right? I think CAC was roughly about $285 in Q3. So again, we believe it'll fluctuate within 10%-15% of this range, roughly about $300, right? So we feel if we can maintain our spend, our CAC at current levels, we are in a good spot. The reason why we're in a good spot is because we know at this level of CAC, we'll be able to get payback within approximately six months, and we'll also be able to achieve that 3-to-1 ratio over a 36-month period of time.

George Kelly: Okay. Maybe if I could sneak in one more quick one. The updated gross margin target, the long-term target of 70%-75%, how much visibility do you have on that? Are these manufacturing changes and the new products and stuff a big part of it? It's a big jump, so I'm trying to understand your confidence.

Brian Rosin: Yeah, there's two parts. There's one that's on the manufacturing side, and there's the other piece that's on the fulfillment side. In both of those areas, I think we have identified some fairly low-hanging fruit of, as we get more economies of scale, we'll be able to get better pricing on some of those areas. I would say, we haven't figured out how to get to the upper range of that target. It's pretty clear to me how we're going to get towards the bottom part of that range with some work to be done for sure, but fairly straightforward to get there within four to six quarters, I would say.

Again, not specific guidance, but I would expect us to approach the lower range of that 70% number towards the end of next year at some point. Towards the 75%, as the business continues to grow and as we bring on additional capacity, you add some, again, more economies of scale, and on both parts of it, again, manufacturing and logistics. I think that we would be shooting for the upper range eventually, but the lower end is clearer in sight right now.

Operator: Thank you, George. Our next question comes from Kyle Bauser of Titan. Kyle, please go ahead.

Just how have the pricing competitive dynamics been out there? Obviously, you've got a premium price on yours given the superior product, but should we expect continued pricing stability?

Danny Yeung: Yeah, I mean, we haven't seen much price issues for us. I mean, again, we haven't changed our pricing since we've I mean, actually, since we've launched, we've actually had a slight price increase, but we haven't seen any issues in terms of price elasticity or any type of demand, as you see evidenced by the continued growth on a quarterly basis.

Kyle Bauser: Got it. Maybe just around the clinical trials, can you talk a little bit more about how this might be unlocking new segments of the population? Obviously, consumers are getting much smarter, and awareness is certainly building. Do you anticipate results driving kind of new cohorts of consumers or

Danny Yeung: that consumer. We will be able to leverage that in terms of marketing. A lot of marketing and also, like you mentioned, clinicians will be able to prescribe it much more. Very, very positive and hopeful about these trials that are going to be releasing in the first half of 2027.

Kyle Bauser: Excellent. Well, thanks for all the updates.

Operator: Thank you, Kyle. Our last question comes from Alex Hantman of Sidoti. Alex, please go ahead.

Alex Hantman: Thank you, thanks for taking questions. I just wanted to start with repeat orders. They were looking great, 59% of customer billing this quarter. I am curious, as that share grows, how quickly does acquisition marketing come down towards your 35%-50% range, what does that mean for the timing of profitability?

Brian Rosin: Yeah, so the 59% is nice to see. However, if we can continue to invest at the three to one, we would rather keep spending more and more into new customers. So it is a conundrum in that when we spend more on customer acquisition, your percent of new revenue is higher, but that is a great sign for the future with the returns that we have. So, I would again say that profitability is not necessarily a goal. It is inevitable with the math that eventually it just becomes too hard to outrun it, as I mentioned a little bit ago.

So, it is hard to put a timeline on it because we have exceeded kind of where I would have expected us to have been able to spend up to at a CAC that is declining. If that continues, then of course we will continue to do that, at which point you push profitability out. If we start to slow to spend, it brings profitability forward in the nearer term. It is too tricky to try to say specifically when that will happen because we have been exceeding what I would have thought we could have been spending. Again, with new products and all that, we do not know how those are going to impact CAC.

We do not know how it is going to impact overall LTVs and LTRs. We need to get these products launched before we will be able to kind of model into the future more specifically around profitability target. I would expect that the marketing will continue to come down as a percentage of sales, which we saw it already from Q2 to Q3. I would expect that to trend mostly down. There might be some blips here and there, but mostly that will keep trending down to that range that we gave for longer term.

Alex Hantman: Okay, helpful context. Thank you. Speaking of new products, I know IM8 Hydration launches into about 160,000 active subscriptions. It is a big number. I am curious what attach rate would you consider a success in year one if you have a target, and also about how margins might compare to the core products?

Brian Rosin: Alex, from a margin standpoint, just to touch on the margin of those. The margin profile will be very similar to our current business margin, from a product cost standpoint, for sure. From a logistics standpoint, it depends on if we can trade people into a multi-month, or a bigger basket size and attach, whether it is our current products or an Essentials bundle. Or if you are getting a three-month supply of Hydration, for example, that will allow the margin to keep really in line with where we are today.

If we are seeing AOV start to decline, because people are taking more of the one-month supply of Hydration, which is a lower price point out the door than our current assortment, you might see a little bit of margin pressure just on the fulfillment side alone. It costs us more or less the same to ship a product to a consumer if they buy $50 worth as if they pay $100. You will see a bit of pressure potentially, depending on how AOV looks. We will be trying it on the DTC channel for sure to get people into a multipack, which would alleviate that pressure entirely. The retail piece is also the other unknown there.

The retail channel looks different from a margin profile, as you can imagine. Much lower cost on the fulfillment side, much lower cost on the actual ad dollars specific going into retail. As I model it out, I think the margin of the total new products will be very unchanged versus the current. There is going to be some pluses and minuses there, but overall, I would not expect it to be pressured much.

Alex Hantman: Very helpful. Thanks for the color. Last one from us. I know we have spoken about retail at length, but the 2027 bridge also includes about $19 million from marketplace and B2B. I know that is only about 5% of revenue, but I wanted to hear a little bit more about the B2B opportunity looks like and how fast perhaps that could grow from your perspective.

Danny Yeung: Yeah. On the marketplace aspect is like Amazon, B2B, we actually have a lot of other businesses reaching out to us as part of their wellness aspects. Again, it is still a small part of our overall business if you consider next year we are forecasting $400 million. I think the focus will still remain DTC and then retail, and then B2B and marketplace, these are more like ad hoc opportunities that we will pick up.

Alex Hantman: Great. Thank you very much.

Operator: Thank you, Alex. That concludes our question and answer session. I will now turn the call back over to Danny for brief closing remarks.

Danny Yeung: Great. Thank you so much, everyone, for tuning in today. Hopefully it was very insightful. As I mentioned, we have a very detailed shareholder letter and investor deck, that we just pushed online. Yeah, I mean, again, going back to summary-wise, this quarter is another record quarter. We are heading into 2027 with a lot of strength. The revenues are growing, the cash position is growing, our cohorts are growing, with new products. It is very clear to us, at least from a business perspective, that we are reaching stronger momentum on a quarterly and on a monthly basis. Yeah, so we cannot be more excited about where the business is headed.

So, thank you, everyone, for tuning in, and look forward to chatting with everyone in the next quarter.

AAA predicts that 73 million Americans will travel by car for Thanksgiving between Nov. 24 and Nov. 30. Google Maps is ready to accompany travelers on their journeys with four new features just in time for holiday travel near and far.

In a press release, Google said it’s rolling out four new Ask Maps features that make it easy to create itineraries, find available appointments, and search your saved lists. Here’s what to know about the latest features coming to Google Maps.

Google has made it easy to build step-by-step itineraries and get real-time route details when you pull up directions. You can use Ask Maps to plan simple tasks, like a day of holiday shopping, or more complex plans, like a multi-day road trip with stops along the way.

Also: I tested Google Maps vs. Waze to find the best navigation app

You can get a day-by-day schedule with tips and numbered map pins for each stop, which makes it easy to visualize your plan. You can also share your itinerary with friends and family, or export it to Google Docs. It’s like being your own trip planner without outsourcing the work to a travel agent. To access your itinerary, ask Maps to pull it up, or look for the “itinerary” badge in your chat history. This way, you can see real-time details like live traffic conditions, whether a place is open, and more.

Maps can help you stay ahead. You can now pull up directions with helpful tips before you go, tailored to your route and plan. These include tips on where to park or charge your car, as well as real-time updates on conditions such as weather, potential delays, tolls, and more.

We’re heading into the most wonderful (and busiest) time of year for travel and shopping, and Google wants to reduce your stress. Thanks to new agentic capabilities, you can have Ask Maps find beauty, pet care, auto, and home repair appointments online and call local businesses for you. Ask, “Find a 4 p.m. hair appointment near me,” and Ask Maps will show you open slots at nearby businesses so you can book and go. It’s that easy.

If you’re playing host for the holidays, Google will help you show off all your town’s favorite spots. Now you can use Ask Maps to find saved places on your lists. Ask things like, “Which spots saved in my lists have availability for 6 people in the next half-hour?” Ask Maps scans across your lists and checks live availability so you can pick a place and just go.

Also: I’m an Apple Maps fan, but I switch to Google Maps for these 3 tasks

Updates begin rolling out today on Android and iOS, and Ask Maps is also expanding to 30 countries across Europe, including Spain, Germany, and the UK. Ask Maps will now be available in more than 200 countries and territories. Travel itineraries and list search will be available everywhere Ask Maps is offered, while route tips and appointment locating will first launch in the US, with more regions to follow soon, according to Google.

#3116. I’ve Used VSCO’s Lightroom Rival Desktop Editor and It’s Great for Creatives

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

VSCO might be popular for iPhone photography, but its Studio Pro has rival Adobe firmly in its sights.

Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe

Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe

VSCO is best known these days for its iPhone and Android editing app that makes pics look all cool and analog. But the company is launching its first stand-alone desktop photo editor for Mac, called VSCO Studio Pro, bringing its famous filmic presets—and a wealth of editing tools. I’ve used it, and while it’s not yet my sole image-editing solution, it’s great for getting those dreamy vintage vibes out of your photos.

The desktop app will be immediately familiar to any photographer who’s spent any time in Lightroom or Capture One. There are exposure, contrast, highlight, and shadow sliders along with color sliders for white balance or individual color adjustments. It’s par for the course for any raw image editor.

VSCO’s wide range of color presets has always been where it shines the brightest. Numbering just north of 200, Studio Pro packs in all the presets, from color classics like the company’s A1-10 range to a wealth of black-and-white options and a host of presets designed to emulate real film stocks like Kodak Gold or Fuji Velvia. VSCO says these are modeled on real scans of these film stocks to make them as authentic as possible.

It’s the presets that I love the most in VSCO’s app. Years ago, the company sold its presets as a downloadable Lightroom preset pack, which I have used in my photography workflow almost daily for the past 13 years, and their look is identical here. While it hasn’t sold the Lightroom preset pack in about a decade, VSCO’s Studio Pro app finally lets photographers achieve those same looks in desktop editing.

With Studio Pro, VSCO clearly has its sights on Lightroom. While Adobe is increasingly filling its services with various generative AI tools that radically alter your image’s content, VSCO is taking a more stripped-back approach that focuses on the creative side of color and exposure adjustments.

It’s still quite bare-bones at launch, with several features I need for my own photography missing, like masking. I can’t make selective edits to my images—like using a gradient to tone down the highlights only in the sky. Apparently this is coming soon, as are bloom and halation tools, which are already in the app, but grayed out with a “soon” marker next to them. Ditto the spot removal tool for cleaning up dust or sensor spots.

The big thing for me, though, comes down to cataloging and archiving of my images. I have several terabytes of images cataloged in my Lightroom library, available to edit on any device I sign in on — including phone, tablet or desktop. While VSCO will have some basic organization options within the Studio Pro app (grouping images into “Projects”—again, coming soon), it’s not as full-featured as Lightroom’s archiving system. I worry that once I’m working with thousands of images across multiple photoshoots, things will quickly become cluttered and difficult to navigate. Time will tell.

I don’t imagine VSCO’s app will necessarily be the first choice for working pros who need strict cataloging, backups and remote access. I count myself in that category, and for me Lightroom’s cloud storage remains the biggest reason to stay with Adobe, while others swear by Capture One for its Sessions-based filing system and its tethered shooting workflow.

By contrast, I see VSCO Studio Pro appealing more to enthusiast photographers who want to efficiently add real creative flair to their images and don’t necessarily want to spend on the commercial tools, cloud storage, or AI options offered by Adobe.
