#3066. Microsoft says its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Microsoft announced two new AI models at Ignite 2026 that promise impressive performance for much lower cost. They could reshape its relationship with OpenAI and Anthropic for good.

At today’s Microsoft Ignite 2026 keynote, the company introduced two new frontier AI models built for what the company describes as “everyday” coding tasks. But there’s a bigger story: what these models might mean for Microsoft’s AI costs and its dependence on OpenAI.

Microsoft claims its MAI Code 2 model shows 96% of Claude Opus 5.5 performance at 5% of Opus 5.5’s price.

Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

Microsoft says MAI Code 2 offers comparable performance to GPT-6.1 Sol or Opus 5.5 at a fraction of the cost. Microsoft’s Code 2 Flash model is comparable to the lower-end GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5, also at considerably lower cost.

This doesn’t mean that those of us who pay for $100/month subscriptions will suddenly get the equivalent for five bucks. Instead, these are usage-based metrics based on API usage.

It’s also important to understand that the benchmarks are all Microsoft-provided. Performance numbers may well differ once the models undergo independent performance tests.

Throughout Satya Nadella’s keynote, Microsoft showed slides referencing a wide range of foundation models that are intended to work with Copilot and other Microsoft offerings. Microsoft famously has a multi-billion-dollar investment in OpenAI dating back to 2023, and has built many of its products and services around OpenAI intellectual property.

But now, Redmond is benchmarking its internally built models against Anthropic and OpenAI offerings, and also touting that it’s integrating these new models as optional choices for GitHub Copilot, Microsoft 365, and Fabric.

Also: 75% of developers I surveyed prefer Claude Code over Codex

One thing that Nadella made clear in today’s keynote is how central AI is becoming in everything Microsoft does. Nearly all of those AI operations previously involved the company paying some token fees back to the frontier model providers or customers doing the same thing.

But with high-performing models of its own, Microsoft may become substantially less dependent on outside model providers, especially for the incredible volume of fairly basic and routine AI requests that occur across the company’s vast product line.

If you think back over the history of agentic work models like ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork, you may recall that they originated as agentic coding tools. As users adopted the coding harnesses in Claude Code and OpenAI Codex to off-label productivity applications, the AI companies noticed and packaged work-centric agentic tools that were more non-programmer-friendly.

Also: I let ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork loose on my files – only one made me nervous

There’s a lot of similarity between a coding agent and a work agent, including understanding a complex environment, using tools to change things, and producing reliable results. Coding turns out to be a very good environment for developing and testing these capabilities, particularly because code output is highly measurable. Coding agents are effective training grounds for non-coding work agents.

This becomes really interesting in today’s announcement. Along with Code 2 and Code 2 Flash, Microsoft announced MAI Work Flash, which it describes as having been derived from Code 2 Flash. Work Flash can help generate formulas in Excel, work with documents and instructions in Word, track decisions and extract useful information from Teams, and more.

Think about the level of intelligence these tasks are demanding from the AI models. Not that much. As long as the models are good enough, they’ll be good enough.

If Microsoft can reduce its expenses and use reliable models at a much lower price, the company itself will be able to save quite a bit of money across its entire software economy, while at the same time maintaining a deeper level of vertical integration and, therefore, control.

Let’s run some hypothetical numbers. Let’s say a company is spending $0.01 per AI request, which, with these new models, can drop down to $0.001 per request.

Also: Want to try ChatGPT Wallet? Read OpenAI’s liability disclaimer very carefully first

A company with a daily inference cost of a million dollars (a company like Microsoft, for example) could drop that daily cost to about $100,000. Add that up across a year, and the change in models could save $325 million annually.

A million here, a million there. Pretty soon, you’re talking real money.

There’s no direct evidence that Microsoft is trying to produce replacement models for the frontier providers’ offerings. But it is an interesting and compelling story if we look at Microsoft developing its own engines for the software it sells.

Microsoft says the numbers it’s reporting at are using a 50% introductory discount. That’s why I measured against $0.001 per request instead of $0.0005 per request above.

Benchmark selection could be cherry-picking. The numbers are impressive. But as we all know, there are lies, damned lies, and benchmark results. I’m fairly sure Microsoft isn’t padding these numbers too much, because it benefits from the new models more than even its own customers, but still. It’s an open issue.

The company also described clearly that these new models are not designed to handle the most challenging agentic and research workloads. You’re probably not going to use them to solve a decades-old mathematics challenge. But you’re very likely to use them to reformat your PowerPoint.

Speaking of reformatting your PowerPoint, Microsoft also emphasized that these new models did unusually well on visualization assignments. That’s a very good fit for not only UI design challenges but also graphics and slide production.

#3065. Disney Imagineers Have Built AI-Powered ‘Star Wars’ Alien Audio-Animatronics With AWS

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Semi-exclusive: Three original Anzellan characters with distinct personalities will interact with guests in Disney parks.

Disney is celebrating 75 years of its Imagineers, who have been amusing and delighting guests with audio-animatronic characters since talking parrots debuted in the Enchanted Tiki Room at Disneyland. But today, new robotic characters are being powered up with artificial intelligence.

In partnership with Amazon Web Services, AI has helped Walt Disney Imagineering create three new Anzellan animatronics that will live bring a Disney theme park retail space to life, presumably in Star Wars: Galaxy’s Edge.

Anzellans are a race of tiny humanoid creatures that repair droids and starships in the Star Wars universe. They include Babu Frik in Star Wars: Episode IX — The Rise of Skywalker and the droidsmiths introduced in season 3 of The Mandalorian. The droidsmiths take on larger roles in The Mandalorian and Grogu, helping Baby Yoda rescue Din Djarin from the Hutts.

The new Anzellan animatronics built by Disney Imagineers use AWS cloud and AI capabilities in order to “understand the scene around them,” Kyle Laughlin, SVP of Walt Disney Imagineering R&D and Technology and Engineering, tells me.

“If you imagine walking into an experiential retail store, you now will be greeted not by a pre-scripted animation or interaction, but a totally personalized experience where each of these Anzellans [has] their own personalities,” Laughlin says, adding that they’ll be attuned to how many people are nearby and whether they’re children or adults.

The animatronic aliens will be able to interact with guests, right down to commenting on people who are wearing a birthday button or even a certain Star Wars T-shirt. Speaking with these animatronics will give guests the same experience they would have when meeting a character walking around the park, Laughlin adds. They also play off each other and react to what each other are doing, with no one controlling them behind the scenes.

The three audio-animatronic prototypes, which will make their first appearance during AWS re:Invent in Las Vegas on Nov. 30 before moving into one of the Disney Parks, are named Vilo Vele, Kado Bre’a and Jibu Bre’a.

They’re original characters created just for this project in partnership with Lucasfilm and the filmmakers, and they all have their own personalities devised by the Imagineers. Vilo is the boss, Kado is the droidsmith mechanic who wants to be the center of attention and Jibu, though Kado’s twin, is the shy one. The animatronics speak a mix of English (or Galactic Basic in-universe) and Anzellan, as they do in the Star Wars movies and TV series, and have hundreds of thousands of prerecorded lines of dialogue to draw from when talking to guests and each other.

Samira Panah Bakhtiar, AWS general manager of Telco, Media & Entertainment, Games, Advertising and Sports, tells me this is “one of the most delightful examples” of physical AI.

“When you talk about physical AI, it’s AI that perceives, it reasons and it acts in the real world,” she says. “It’s not just AI on a screen.”

Bakhtiar says Disney was able to use both AWS cloud computing and AI tools to “get from idea to implementation several magnitudes faster than they would have otherwise,” with Laughlin specifying it took “mere months.”

AWS staff used a coding agent called Kiro that built their creative briefs into software, which was then reviewed and approved by humans. Imagineers also used the Amazon Bedrock fully managed AI service, which allows them to choose between all the biggest AI models, including those from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta.

“We’re providing Amazon Bedrock to the Imagineering team to be able to leverage the right models that they need at the right time to be able to really enhance those character experiences,” Bakhtiar tells me. “From multimodal models that focus on voice to world models, to large language models. The point is that they are able to get the right tool at the right time and then do so in a way that’s secure, resilient, performant and globally available.”

Bakhtiar says AWS is continuing to work with Disney, though the next project is under wraps.

“The future of entertainment is going to be highly personalized,” she says. “It’s going to be multidimensional, and it’s going to be more interactive than ever. And I think this is an incredible example of that coming to life.”

Disney had previously teamed up with Nvidia on robotics and AI to bring a robot version of fan-favorite Frozen character Olaf to life so he can wander around Disneyland Paris and Hong Kong Disneyland, and is also now exploring robots paired with AI that could guide guests throughout Disneyland parking lots.

“You can imagine an entire franchise of characters working and interacting with one another,” says Laughlin. “We’ve done a number of things in the Star Wars universe. We’re just getting started in Frozen, and we have a wealth of IP that we can mine to bring those characters to our guests as fast as possible.”

Correction, 3:48 p.m. ET: The original version of this story incorrectly stated who used the Kiro coding agent to build the software. It was staff from AWS.

#3063. 6 Stocks Set to Cash In on the Grand Theft Auto VI Launch Boom

Take-Two Interactive is the obvious winner, but it's not the only company that will benefit.

By Geoffrey Seiler – Nov 18, 2026 at 6:04PM EST

Grand Theft Auto is one of the most iconic video game franchises on the planet, and its newest edition, Grand Theft Auto VI, or GTA6, has been called the most anticipated video game in history. All five previous versions of the game have been hits, and it's been more than 13 years since Grand Theft Auto V was released in September 2013. With an estimated $1 billion budget, a lot is riding on the game, and early signs are that it is set to deliver.

A day before its launch, the game had nearly $1.7 billion in preorders, and it was already drawing rave reviews. The game was already atop Metacritic's all-time gaming leaderboard with a score of 99, which had only happened one other time back in 1998, with Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

With excitement building, let's look at six stocks set to cash in on Grand Theft Auto VI.

As the developer of the game, Take-Two Interactive (TTWO +6.22%) is the biggest winner. It's already closing in on $2 billion in orders, and management has projected Q3 net bookings for its fiscal Q3 to reach $3.35 billion to $3.5 billion, about double from a year ago.

The key going forward, though, will be how the company monetizes the game over the long term, through online multiplayer extensions and recurring consumer spending. The up-front sales are great, but that is just part of the story.

Sony (SONY -0.04%), which makes the PlayStation gaming console, is also set to be a big winner. About 75% of preorders have been for PlayStation versions of the game. The success of the game could not only drive sales of its PS5 and higher-margin PS5 Pro, but also give it a take rate on all digital software downloads and in-game microtransactions made through the PlayStation Store.

Both Walmart (WMT -0.13%) and Target (TGT +4.01%) should also benefit from the launch of GTA6. Now, these retailers will not be selling physical discs; instead, physical boxed copies of the game will contain a digital download code. However, collectors still like to get boxed copies for the artwork and physical inserts like maps, while it's also a better gift presentation for the upcoming holidays.

Importantly, it can increase foot traffic to their stores, which can also lead to other impulse purchases that typically don't happen online.

Big video game launches are also often accompanied by strong sales of gaming peripherals. This can be a revenue growth driver for a company like Turtle Beach (TBCH +1.55%), which holds a roughly 40% share of the U.S. gaming headset market. It has also expanded into other accessories, such as controllers, chargers, and simulation gear.

Gamers tend to upgrade or replace equipment during big new game launches. The company also has strong retail distribution, with its items placed near popular games.

While all these companies could see a lift from the sales of physical items, Reddit (RDDT -0.41%) could see a strong benefit from increased community engagement on its platform around GTA6. It's common for its platform to have dedicated gaming communities, and with the launch of a game the size and scope of Grand Theft Auto VI, millions of users will likely flood gaming subreddits to share clips, potential easter eggs, map theories, and gameplay discoveries.

Young, predominantly male gamers are a highly desirable demographic for many advertisers, and brands that cater to this segment will likely be looking to spend to capture their attention for what is not just a video game launch, but a true cultural phenomenon. Reddit, meanwhile, is in a unique position to command strong ad prices, given the concentration of hyperengaged eyeballs on its gaming subreddits.

#3062. Which Laptops Last the Longest? Check Out the Laptops I’ve Tested With the Best Battery Life

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

As part of our video series Holiday Office Hours From the Labs, I share laptop recommendations and explain why battery life surged in 2026.

I can almost guarantee that your next laptop will run longer on battery power than whatever you’re currently using. We’ve seen a huge leap in laptop battery life in recent years, to the point where getting 20 or more hours on a single charge isn’t uncommon. This year alone, the average battery life of the laptops we’ve tested at CNET has increased by more than five hours. And it’s nearly doubled since the start of the decade.

With many of today’s laptops, you can leave the charger at home for days at a time. The longest-lasting laptop I tested this year lasted more than 34 hours!

This increase in battery life is one of the biggest stories in laptops this year. In the laptop episode of our video series Holiday Office Hours From the Labs, I explain what’s behind this surge in battery life and highlight some of the laptops that lasted the longest in testing.

Plus, my colleagues Kyle Kucharski from ZDNET and Joe Osborne from PCMag share their own holiday laptop picks. Kyle looks at Apple’s entry-level MacBook Neo and its imitators, and Joe breaks down what to look for in a budget gaming laptop.

Unlike raw performance, where the more you spend, the more you get, lengthy battery life can be found just as easily in a budget laptop as in an expensive, high-end powerhouse. And, in fact, less powerful components and lower screen resolutions can give cheaper laptops an edge in battery life.

The biggest factor behind longer battery life in laptops is the advancement in mobile processors. They’ve become much more power efficient, and in the case of Apple’s and Qualcomm’s chips, they’re based on an architecture other than the traditional x86 instruction set that’s been at the heart of Intel processors since the dawn of the PC era.

Apple’s run of battery-life winners started when it shifted from Intel processors to its own M-series chips. Apple’s M-series processors are based on the Arm architecture, a power-efficient chip architecture found in phones and tablets. Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X-series processors are also Arm-based, and they can be found in the two longest-running laptops we’ve tested: the HP OmniBook 3 16 and OmniBook 5 14. The OmniBook 3 16’s record-setting battery performance earned it a CNET Lab Award for longest battery life.

Intel has made huge strides in processor efficiency with its last two generations of chips: the Core Ultra 200 series developed under the name Lunar Lake, and the Core Ultra 300 series, also known as Panther Lake. Last year, the Lenovo Yoga 9i 2-in-1 Aura Edition became the first Intel laptop to last longer than a day, running for 25 hours, 45 minutes in testing. It’s still the longest-running Intel laptop we’ve tested, but the MSI Prestige 14 Flip AI Plus with Intel’s next-gen Core Ultra X7 358H processor came close with a time of 25 hours, 18 minutes.

Read more: Laptops With the Best Battery Life

Whether Arm or x86, there are two more reasons behind greater processor efficiency and longer laptop battery life. For one, the size of a processor shrinks with every generation. The smaller a processor is and the more tightly packed its components are, the less power is required to flip its tinier transistors on and off. For another, today’s mobile processors feature more flexible designs with a mix of performance and efficiency cores. A processor engages its higher-performance cores only when needed, using the efficiency cores for as many general, everyday tasks as possible, so your laptop stays cool and quiet and runs longer.

For more, you can read my Labs exclusive on the huge increase in laptop battery life this year and check out the video above for my holiday laptop picks and those from my colleagues.

#3061. Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

With Agent 365 Business Analytics, Microsoft could reshape enterprise spending, but there's a critical difference between estimated value and money saved.

We all know AI can get expensive. But does that expense result in real business value? That’s the trillion-dollar question Microsoft aims to answer with today’s introduction of Agent 365 Business Analytics.

Also: Microsoft says its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost

Earlier this year, Microsoft introduced Agent 365, its tool for tracking agents the way an HR department would normally track human employees. With Agent 365 Business Analytics, Microsoft is attempting to build an accounting system for AI labor. The system attempts to calculate the economic value of the work performed by agents compared with what the agents cost, and then provide a return on investment estimate.

If it works, this is some very cool stuff. Microsoft is trying to map labor-market economics onto AI usage data to create value estimates.

Also: Work IQ is Microsoft’s big bet on agent-first enterprise IT, and I have questions

To do so, it uses real labor-costing information, including data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, the O*NET database from the US Department of Labor, and its own LinkedIn Occupational Graph.

This data, along with data gathered from Agent 365, is aggregated into analysis intended to answer:

The goal is to provide a comprehensive picture of AI spend against value produced.

Software accounting is long established and straightforward. We measure subscription fees, cost per seat, compute costs, burden costs (like floor space and other infrastructure), and more. But AI work doesn’t fit that model, making it very hard to quantify value.

Instead, Agent 365 Business Analytics measures cost both relative to human labor and in terms of technological expense. For example, it might look at a task and determine how much human effort that task would normally take, and then price that effort based on prevailing common labor rates.

Then, it might factor in how much of the task was actually done by a human vs. how much was contributed by an AI, along with the estimated value of the AI’s contribution. Then it mixes in the actual AI processing cost (whether in subscriptions, tokens, on-premises infrastructure, and cloud support).

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI – what’s new

What comes out is a hybrid labor estimate that combines human contribution, human-replacement savings, AI costs, and then potentially AI savings over human costs. It sounds positively Orwellian. But the bottom line is that companies really haven’t been able to understand the AI bottom line.

There’s a catch. All these numbers are estimates. In its blog post, Redmond specifically says, “Assisted hours are a directional estimate of work AI helped complete, not measured time saved or financial return.”

In other words, what Agent 365 Business Analytics estimates might not actually line up with real-world experience or expenses. It’s also possible that AI work might have been assigned because there was AI to do the work, not that the AI was saving company labor costs with every token processed.

In other words, Microsoft may be able to tell you the economic value of AI-assisted work, but it can’t demonstrate definitively that the company saved any real money.

Also: 5 reasons your company needs a chief AI officer in 2026

I find it particularly telling that this is from the company that makes PowerPoint. Because now, with Agent 365 Business Analytics, it’s entirely possible that you could produce economic dashboards that look really, really impressive, but are entirely irrelevant to real life.

That’s not to say the product is useless. But it does go to the idea that you will have to be quite disciplined in how you interpret the results and how much stock you put in them for decision-making. It is one source of possible truth, not the source of absolute truth.

Microsoft has been investing for decades to build out the core infrastructure of enterprise computing. AI isn’t any different when it comes to the company’s overall mission.

With Agent 365 and the company’s related offerings, Microsoft wants to help you:

This means the company doesn’t necessarily have to provide you with the AI model to help you run your enterprise. With integration with offerings from OpenAI, Anthropic, Salesforce, Google, Databricks, Snowflake, and others, the company doesn’t even have to provide the apps or SaaS capabilities.

But if it can get in there and manage your plumbing, help you control costs, and be the HR operation for your AI workforce, Microsoft could own a central piece of your business’s operations.

Maybe fans want to learn about the early days of Haymitch Abernathy, but the sixth Hunger Games movie stretches the franchise thin

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Rewatching the original “The Hunger Games” this week before seeing the new prequel “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,” I was struck by how much Jennifer Lawrence’s powerful, empathetic performance carries what is otherwise a fairly generic dystopian game-of-death movie. If “The Hunger Games” is operating on a slightly higher level than other similar movies, that’s almost entirely thanks to Lawrence’s compelling performance as Katniss Everdeen, the steely teenager who eventually leads a rebellion against the tyrannical government of Panem.

As has been widely reported, Lawrence shows up again in “Sunrise on the Reaping,” although her appearance is so brief that it hardly makes an impression. Instead, the movie focuses on relative newcomer Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy, the character played as an adult by Woody Harrelson in the first four “Hunger Games” movies. Like the 2023 prequel “The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes,” the new movie suffers from its lack of a Lawrence-caliber star who can hold the audience’s attention through yet another iteration of the overly familiar titular tournament.

Directed by Francis Lawrence, who helmed four of the previous five “Hunger Games” movies, “Sunrise on the Reaping” is competently produced and occasionally exciting, with an admirably downbeat finale. But it’s hard to shake the feeling that it’s entirely redundant, filling in gaps that didn’t need to be filled, just for the sake of returning to the world of an enduringly popular franchise.

Set 24 years before the events of “The Hunger Games,” “Sunrise on the Reaping” follows Haymitch as he competes in the 50th annual edition of the event that pits children from the 12 districts of Panem against each other in a gruesome death match. This year’s edition, known as the second “quarter quell,” requires each district to send twice as many tributes as usual, so Haymitch is joined by three others from his home in District 12.

Haymitch is a headstrong rebel who’s picked for the Hunger Games not by chance, but because he dared to stick up for his girlfriend, Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak), when she was being roughed up by the militaristic Peacekeepers. One of Lenore Dove’s favorite things to say is that nothing is inevitable, but anyone who’s seen the previous “Hunger Games” movies knows that it actually is inevitable that Haymitch will win the Hunger Games, and that he won’t be able to topple Panem’s totalitarian regime.

That takes a lot of the suspense out of “Sunrise on the Reaping,” even though author Suzanne Collins (who adapts her book along with screenwriters Billy Ray and Michael Lesslie) finds ways to generate excitement along the way to the predetermined outcome. Haymitch teams up with younger versions of some recognizable characters, including previous Hunger Games winners, to attempt to sabotage the games, and his path to victory isn’t straightforward or simple.

Still, much of the movie involves the same kind of battles and threats that Katniss faced multiple times in the earlier installments.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Like “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes,” which takes place during the 10th Hunger Games and provides an origin story for Panem’s diabolical President Coriolanus Snow (played here by Ralph Fiennes), “Sunrise on the Reaping” fills in some details on the history of Panem, including the evolution of the Hunger Games themselves.

Lawrence gives this time period a 1970s feel, with lots of wide-lapel outfits and groovy upholstery patterns, and the Hunger Games are not quite as sophisticated as in Katniss’ era, although much more so than in the more distant past. The setting allows Collins to embrace the brutality of the dystopian world while preserving the hopeful ending of the original four movies.

Zada is a bit bland as Haymitch, but he captures enough of Harrelson’s vocal mannerisms that the two versions of the character feel connected. The other younger incarnations of existing characters are a mixed bag, from Kieran Culkin’s failure to channel Stanley Tucci’s effortless smarm as host Caesar Flickerman to Elle Fanning’s uncanny recreation of Elizabeth Banks’ flamboyant stylist Effie Trinket.

Some of those appearances are little more than fan service, but they give the sense of Panem as a wider society, beyond Katniss’ personal connections. Longtime fans may be satisfied just to spend more time in Panem, but “Sunrise on the Reaping” rarely establishes itself as a distinctive story worth telling on its own.

The only time when “Sunrise on the Reaping” has any bite is in its extended epilogue, after the Hunger Games have concluded. That’s when the true price that Haymitch has to pay becomes clear, and the filmmakers don’t hold back on torturing the young man who’s already been through such a horrific ordeal. It’s the same darkness that defined the final hour of “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes,” here focused on a character more deserving of sympathy.

That bracing sorrow comes only after nearly two hours of the Hunger Games’ greatest hits, and it doesn’t make as much of an impact as it could, given what viewers know about Haymitch’s ultimate fate. That’s the problem with any prequel, and “Sunrise on the Reaping” never quite overcomes it. Even when their storytelling faltered, the original “Hunger Games” movies always had Jennifer Lawrence to fall back on. By the time she finally shows up here, there’s not much she can do.

“The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” opens Nov. 20 in theaters

#3059. Palo Alto Networks: Accelerating Growth and a $4.5 Billion Bet on the Future of Cybersecurity

Demand has never been stronger for the cybersecurity specialist.

By Danny Vena, CPA – Nov 18, 2026 at 6:14PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Palo Alto Networks ›

A quick look at the headlines is all it takes to understand the unprecedented need for robust cybersecurity. The emergence of next-generation artificial intelligence (AI)-powered threats has emboldened hackers, and the frequency of attacks has risen to new heights.

With that as a backdrop, investors watched closely as Palo Alto Networks (PANW +9.90%) released its quarterly financial report. Shareholders were pleased to find that the company has risen to the challenge, as robust demand has fueled record growth. Palo Alto also made a sizable investment to ensure that enterprises can adopt AI securely, regardless of what models they use.

For its fiscal 2027 first quarter (ended Oct. 31), Palo Alto Networks delivered record revenue that grew 39% year over year to $3.44 billion, driven primarily by robust growth in its Next-Generation Security annual recurring revenue (NGS ARR). The company also generated adjusted net income of $881 million and adjusted earnings per diluted share (EPS) of $1.05, up 33% and 13%, respectively.

To give those numbers context, analysts' consensus estimates called for revenue of $3.31 billion and adjusted EPS of $0.97, so Palo Alto Networks easily scaled expectations.

It isn't just the current quarter that looks strong. Remaining performance obligation (RPO) -- contractually obligated revenue that hasn't yet been earned -- grew 35% year over year to $21 billion, building a strong foundation for future growth.

Palo Alto Networks' customer metrics were equally compelling, as its net retention rate remained above 120% for its platform customers. Put another way, existing customers are spending 20% more than in the prior-year quarter.

Not only did Palo Alto Networks surprise to the upside, but it also signaled strong growth ahead, as evidenced by its robust outlook. For the fiscal second quarter, management is guiding for revenue of roughly $3.53 billion, or year-over-year growth of roughly 36%.

Investors were particularly inspired by the company's full-year guidance. For fiscal 2027, management is guiding for total revenue of $14.5 billion, up about 26% year over year, with NGS ARR of $11.5 billion, also up 26%. Given management’s tendency to underpromise and overdeliver, that forecast will likely rise over time.

In a surprise announcement, Palo Alto Networks revealed that it will shell out $4.5 billion to acquire Applied Compute, a leading platform for post-training and inference of open-weight AI models. This will allow Palo Alto to "help enterprises adopt AI securely, whether they choose open-weight models, closed frontier models, or both," according to the announcement.

Even as demand remains high, cybersecurity stocks have swooned as technology issues have fallen. Ahead of its Q1 report, Palo Alto Networks shares declined nearly 19% from their early October peak.

However, some investors will still balk at Palo Alto Networks' premium valuation, as the stock currently sells for 82 times forward earnings and 70 times next year's expected earnings. Historically, investors tend to reward high-growth stocks with premium valuations thanks to their consistently above-average, uh, growth.

I'm a firm believer in the old adage "You get what you pay for." Management has shown an uncanny knack for stoking Palo Alto's impressive growth, and recent technological advances make cybersecurity more important than ever.

That's why I'm confident in saying Palo Alto Networks is a buy.

First, Microsoft: At its Ignite developer conference on Tuesday, Microsoft introduced seven new AI models. They include MAI Cyber 2 Flash, MAI Code 2, MAI Image 2.7 and Dragon Copilot Transcribe — models meant to help with tasks in cybersecurity, coding, image generation and transcription.

It’s clear from Microsoft’s marketing that it is aiming to position its new tech as a cheaper alternative to OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s leading models, with many of these significantly cheaper to run at the enterprise level. While these new models might be useful for AI power users, they are far from most of the AI industry’s mind this week. The company also released new ROI tracking tools for companies monitoring their AI spend.

AI-powered workspaces are tech companies’ latest focus, as the industry still struggles to perfect adoption. Microsoft has just put its offering into the ring.

During the keynote for the company’s Ignite conference on Tuesday, CEO Satya Nadella announced Copilot Workspaces, a collaborative, “multiplayer” surface for Copilot’s agentic capabilities.

The product, available in Frontier for now, is similar to OpenAI’s ChatGPT Space and several new Anthropic features, including Whiteboard and Sheets, which essentially merge the work tools you’re used to using with an agentic framework.

“As the evolution of Copilot Notebooks, it’s where people and agents build on each other’s work,” Microsoft said. “An agent drafts a section of a document, and you review. You leave a comment, and an agent picks it up.”

Microsoft also announced Autopilot, a sort of counterpoint agent to Copilot that “can watch Teams channels, follow up on emails, run recurring work, and manage a project — without waiting for a prompt,” as Microsoft described.

In a demo video during the keynote, the agent appeared to function similarly to OpenAI’s Dots, but for work — employees can tag their Autopilot “like a colleague,” Microsoft said, and assign it tasks.

Also: 4 ways Anthropic’s new Claude Sheets beat using a Google Sheets connector

Speaking of trust, however, Microsoft noted that “Autopilot runs on the identity, security, and compliance foundation IT already uses,” and that “each Autopilot has its own Microsoft Entra Agent ID and a named manager,” meaning IT can block it as needed.

“Its sign-ins and actions are logged under its own name, so security teams have a clear audit trail. Powered by Work IQ, it understands how your organization works within existing permissions,” Microsoft said.

The company added that employees will soon “be able to bring their personal Autopilot into Workspaces” as well. The feature is also available in Frontier.

Nadella also announced a few other productivity features, including a “command center” called Today that spans email, calendar, meetings, tasks, and threads in Teams. Currently in private preview in Outlook and the Copilot app, it includes a personalized briefing and a feed of priorities that updates throughout the day.

“The draft is written and ready for you to edit; the schedule change is already proposed; and the forgotten follow-up is waiting for you to send it, complete with context so you can catch up quickly,” Microsoft said of the feature, which sounds like an agentic briefing-cum-morning-assistant.

Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now – but many get no time to upskill

Microsoft also announced that Home, now generally available, unifies Chat and Cowork into a singular starting point. That’s similar to Anthropic’s recent consolidation of its chat and agentic Cowork offerings, demonstrating an overall trend toward simplification in workplace AI.

While more companies are finally starting to see a return on their AI investment, agents are still expensive and can quickly rack up costs when unsupervised.

Microsoft announced a few tools to track this at Ignite: Agent 365 Business Analytics and Agent 365 Cost Management.

Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

Agent 365, which Microsoft announced last year, is the company’s observability platform. Microsoft said Business Analytics, in Frontier Public today, provides insights on what a company is spending on AI and why, and where it’s paying off, as well as forecasts future costs. In a demo during the keynote, Microsoft showed how admins can see when specific agents’ costs have spiked recently and what (human) employee to notify as a result.

“It starts with a new way to measure your investment: in work completed, not simply tokens,” Microsoft said. “It analyzes the tasks, how long that work typically takes a person, and the share Cowork performed, providing a sophisticated view of the hours your intelligence supports and what the work is worth.”

Cost Management lets IT see where teams are using AI down to the model.

“Leaders can set spending policies, limits, and proactive alerts and control which models are available,” Microsoft said. Anthropic released a similar tool last month, though it was focused more on making seats as efficient as possible on Teams and Enterprise plans.

If you're looking for a new phone this Black Friday, you may be inclined to pick the latest models. They're newer, after all, and have the latest hardware and software that phone companies offer. But what if I told you that picking up an older phone might be a better option — especially if you're not looking to spend a lot of money?

The real truth is that you're not going to miss out on much when you buy last year's flagship, or even a flagship from the year before. In fact, you might even end up with a device better than some of the best cheap phones that are currently on sale — for the simple reason that these are flagships that haven't been compromised by price.

Don't believe me? Here are five reasons why buying older phones is the better option during the Black Friday sales.

If you look at the cost of the latest flagship phones, you'll notice one thing they all have in common: they're expensive. Even if you do manage to get hold of those phones with some kind of discount, you're still going to be paying several hundred dollars — if not more. Older phones don't really have that issue.

The thing about phones is that releasing a new model doesn't magically make the previous generation disappear. Carriers and retailers lower the price to try and sell off inventory and during Black Friday that strategy gets turned up to 11.

For example, at the time of writing buying the Motorola Razr 2026 at Best Buy will cost you $799 — the full retail price. But last year's Motorola Razr 2025 is $250 less at $549. Likewise, Amazon is selling the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 7 for $1,299, whereas the Z Fold 8 Ultra is currently $1,749.

If you've looked at a new phone and thought "how is this any different from the last one?," you're not alone. Plenty of criticism has been leveled at phone companies for seemingly doing the bare minimum with each new generation, and customers realized that pretty quickly. So if the old one is basically the same as the new one, why does it matter which one you buy?

Our entire staff spends hundreds of hours looking at deals to find the best values. Sign up for our newsletter to get the biggest savings on the hottest products sent to you directly.

At the time of writing, the Galaxy S25 Ultra can be purchased for $859, though it has gone as low as $729 in the past. Meanwhile, an unlocked Galaxy S26 Ultra with no carrier obligations is on sale for $971. If you don't care about the few changes that have been made, then you can spend that extra money on something more important. Those savings could go toward some new accessories, or just your usual monthly expenses.

A new chipset could make major differences to how a phone performs. That's true to an extent, but it's not as though we're seeing gargantuan leaps in performance every single year.

Using the Galaxy S26 Ultra and S25 Ultra as an example again, you can see that the switch from a Snapdragon 8 Elite to the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 is noticeable. Benchmarking results show a rise in computing performance, especially in multi-core testing. The same is true for graphics performance, with an increase to the raw performance score and the average framerate. But how much does the difference matter?

Looking at numbers can only tell you so much, and having used both phones, I can tell you that the difference isn't noticeable with everyday use. Perhaps if you're a fan of high-octane mobile gaming, or you tend to do a lot of performance-heavy tasks on your phone, then sure, better performance may be needed. Likewise, the S26 Ultra lasted an extra 103 minutes in our battery test, no doubt thanks to the extra energy efficiency of the newer hardware.

Is that enough to warrant the extra price? Possibly not, especially if that money could be better spent elsewhere.

In the past, anyone buying an older phone had to contend with the fact the phone may run out of official software support before they were done with it. Not only does this mean you miss out on newly-released software features, loss of security updates meant your phone was more vulnerable to attacks and other security threats — not to mention the fact that you'll eventually stop being able to use your favorite apps.

These days that's much less of a concern. Companies like Google and Samsung have pledged several years of software support on their devices — with up to seven years support on flagships. Likewise, Apple typically offers five to six years of iOS updates on all devices, and makes a point of releasing critical security updates years after other software support has dried up.

Plus, you'd be surprised at how many phone features are purely software-based. There have been instances where AI features on Samsung and Pixel phones started off as exclusive to the newest flagships, but made their way to older phones in a software update.

Extended software support isn't available on all phones, and there are a lot of brands that still offer the bare minimum of two Android updates and three years of security support. Mostly this issue affects budget brands with phones that are typically cheap enough that it makes more sense to buy the latest models — examples include Motorola G Power line and TCL.

Just because you're looking at older phones doesn't mean you should feel pressured into buying used or refurbished models. There are plenty of brand new devices available, but the older the device the less likely you'll be able to find one. That said, there are extra advantages to buying a used device instead.

For starters, used and refurbished phones are often significantly cheaper. Refurbished phones are often a little pricier than standard used phones, because their condition has been restored to the point that they're almost as good as new. Some of them even come with warranties, just to give you the extra piece of mind that things aren't likely to go wrong.

Buying a pre-owned device also means that a single phone is getting a new lease on life, and that has a much lower environmental impact. Rather than buying a brand new phone, which involves mining, manufacturing, shipping and all those other industrial processes, you're saving an older phone from going through that same process in reverse. That's a nice bonus considering you're probably more interested in the lower price tag.

The first Apple e-series phone still has a lot of great qualities. A solid camera, good battery life, Apple Intelligence and the power of the A18 chipset.

This entry-level foldable comes with a large 6.9-inch foldable display, a cover display capable of running full Android apps, an assortment of AI features and compact design.

The iPhone 16 is the oldest phone Apple still sells, and it can be had for slightly less — so long as you're happy being locked to Walmart's Straight Talk MVNO. It's got good cameras and performance, as well as full access to Apple Intelligence.

There's no successor to this super slim phone yet, but its age means it's a little cheaper than other Galaxy phones. Plus, unlike the iPhone Air, this one actually has two cameras to work with.

The iPhone air is slim, lightweight and far more durable than it looks. Not to mention the fact it has all the benefits of owning an iPhone like good performance, camera quality and long software support.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is new, and it's expensive, but last year's model is a good $500 cheaper than the current price. It lacks the crease-free screen and larger battery, but it still offers an excellent viewing experience, battery life and camera performance.

#3055. Thinking About Buying Anthropic’s IPO on Nov. 19? Here’s an AI Stock I’d Consider First (Hint: It’s Not Nvidia or Broadcom).

ASML’s impeccable fundamentals allow investors to rest easy amid AI stock volatility.

By Daniel Foelber – Nov 18, 2026 at 6:15PM EST

Artificial intelligence (AI) stock investors have been on a roller coaster in recent weeks, with far more drops than pops.

The Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +0.42%) is now in a correction -- which is a drop of more than 10% from the highs. The iShares Semiconductor ETF -- which closely tracks the semiconductor industry -- is in a 35.3% drawdown, and leading chip stocks Broadcom (AVGO +3.65%) and Nvidia (NVDA -2.90%) are both down over 30% from their all-time highs.

Red-hot AI spending has pushed once-cash-cow businesses like Amazon, Alphabet, and Meta Platforms into negative free-cash-flow territory. Rising interest rates are making capital more expensive. And Jensen Huang's sudden resignation as CEO of Nvidia leaves the industry without one of its biggest champions.

The timing is bad for Anthropic, which is set to hold its initial public offering (IPO) on Thursday, Nov. 19. Reports indicate Anthropic was eyeing a valuation as high as $2 trillion. But a Nov. 10 press release by Anthropic prices its 825 million shares between $70 and $78 per share. At the midpoint of $74 per share and based on its total share count of 13.09 billion, Anthropic would have a valuation around $968 billion.

Given the downward pressure on AI stocks, some investors may be eyeing Anthropic's IPO as a great buying opportunity for the company behind one of the leading frontier models. But I think semiconductor equipment manufacturer ASML (ASML +0.88%) is an even better way to buy the dip on AI stocks.

Huang's resignation exposed Nvidia's key-person risk. So much of the company's identity, strategy, and even its organizational structure centered around Huang. And his sudden departure is undoubtedly challenging the investment thesis.

Similarly, the frontier models like Anthropic's Claude, OpenAI's ChatGPT, Alphabet's Gemini, and xAI's Grok, owned by Space Exploration Technologies, have shaky moats, as a single upgrade can challenge one model's competitive advantages in a heartbeat.

Meanwhile, hyperscalers like Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet are spending so much on AI so quickly that it's difficult to discern whether those investments will pay off in the long run or prove wasteful.

Uncertain profitability road maps, paired with Nvidia's scandal, have made me even more confident that ASML is the best all-around AI stock to buy for the long term.

Ultimately, ASML doesn't really care if Advanced Micro Devices takes market share from Nvidia or Anthropic grows its lead over OpenAI. Rather, its long-term growth runway depends on increasing demand for next-generation AI chips that must be manufactured on ASML's machines.

ASML has a virtual monopoly on extreme ultraviolet (EUV) machines that are used in the lithography step of chip manufacturing. These machines are needed to mass-produce both logic and memory chips at commercial scale. And the most advanced version of these machines, called high-numerical-aperture (high-NA) EUV, will be needed to make next-generation AI chips.

EUV is making up a larger share of ASML's revenue, but the tech company remains heavily reliant on its deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography systems and aftermarket servicing on existing machines. In its latest quarter, EUV system sales accounted for 35% of net sales -- which puts into context the sheer size of its non-EUV and servicing segments.

ASML being in the relatively early stages of its EUV and high-NA system rollout is music to the ears of long-term investors. ASML spent over 6 billion euros researching and developing EUV over a 17-year period. But many chip fabs have yet to widely adopt high-NA. On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, ASML said that Samsung Electronics will be using high-NA in high-volume manufacturing starting in 2028 -- joining Intel. ASML is also working with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing to unlock the full efficiency benefits of high-NA EUV by 2033.

In the meantime, ASML can't keep up with 2027 or 2028 demand. On its recent third-quarter 2026 earnings call, the company said it is now taking orders for 2029 and 2030 and increasing production to meet customer needs.

If there is an AI spending slowdown, ASML's near-term results will definitely cool off. But it's still incredibly well positioned to capitalize on AI innovation over the long term because chip fabs will need to upgrade their equipment to EUV and high-NA to support advanced-node manufacturing. In the meantime, ASML generates steady revenue from its DUV business, and high-margin cash flow from services for its existing installed base. What's more, ASML isn't dependent on an expensive research and development (R&D) budget because it has already cracked the code on high-NA and is now in the stage of fine-tuning the commercial manufacturing process with chip fabs. Its operating costs are reasonable, and its balance sheet is in impeccable shape -- with ASML exiting its latest quarter with 8.03 billion euros in cash compared to just 1.96 billion euros in long-term debt.

ASML is the exact company long-term investors can rest easy holding during an AI slowdown. The business is extremely high-quality and will produce strong earnings even during a downturn -- albeit at a slower growth rate. ASML can also generate high cash flow to buy back its stock, even if the price gets discounted. And with the growth stock down 23.7% in the last three months, ASML no longer commands as lofty a valuation -- with the price-to-earnings ratio now sitting at a premium but more reasonable 34.7 compared to over 50 a couple of months ago.

ASML is a company built around the strength of its technology, rather than a single key feature or product upgrade. It sits upstream of the AI value chain, making it the perfect bet for investors who believe in a sustainable, gradual AI innovation cycle rather than those looking to capitalize on a boom in a particular bottleneck, such as memory chips.

ASML presents a far more attractive risk-and-reward profile than an Anthropic IPO or setting sail into uncharted waters aboard Nvidia -- a ship that suddenly finds itself without its veteran captain.

#3054. Giving the iPhone Duo a Spin at the Apple Store? Be Sure to Test These Things Out

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Want to test out the iPhone Duo? Here are six things you need to try with it.

Now that the iPhone Duo is in stores, there are plenty of people who are curious about Apple’s first folding device. Foldables are hardly a new sector in the smartphone world, with Samsung leading the charge, but Apple’s entry into the market is a big deal, and the iPhone Duo is a stunner.

If you’re planning on checking out the iPhone Duo at the Apple store, it might be easy to just marvel at how cool it looks, but if you’re considering making this your new phone that’ll be in your pocket all of the time, you’ll probably want to get an idea of how it will be living with this new design. After all, you should be in love with all aspects of the device if you’re going to drop $2,000-plus on it.

Below, we’ve listed a handful of features and things to try out when you’re test-driving the Apple iPhone Duo in the store.

When the Duo was first revealed, Apple showed off a very intriguing animation when you unfold it. Leave it to Apple to make a function so simple look so aesthetically pleasing.

It’ll likely be the first thing you notice when you first open the Duo up to see its inner display, and there’s a good chance you’ll continue to open and close the device to see the effect. At the end of the day, it’s a parlor trick — but a very good one, adding delight to ordinary use.

Read more: The iPhone Duo Crossed 517,000 Folds and Counting in Our Custom Machine

Foldables, well, fold, and they typically come with creases. The Duo has a minimal crease and a matte display, both of which are wins. That said, even the most noticeable creases tend to “disappear” when you’re viewing content — you just get used to them while watching TV shows or YouTube videos. The Duo’s minimal crease should be even easier to ignore.

And let’s not forget about the matte screen. Several foldables ship with glossy displays, but the iPhone Duo will have a less shiny screen, making it easier to view in bright environments without annoying reflections.

The outer passport-size display on the iPhone Duo may be a little awkward for watching videos because of how it crops content to fit the new aspect ratio. Still, it’s handy to prop the phone up in tent mode and watch shows that way. You also have a large inner display to work with, but because of its passport-style design, even that screen has a different aspect ratio than the widescreen format people are used to on regular phones, so there will likely be some letterboxing in videos.

Try watching something with the phone set up in both ways to see if it bothers you enough to dissuade you from buying the phone.

Again, it’s not an iPhone Duo issue but a foldable phone issue — the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the same size and format. The aspect ratio of the display might crop the top or sides of videos, so it’s worth trying out if you expect to watch a lot of full-screen videos.

Like videos, apps on foldables can sometimes appear a little weird, and that could be the case with the iPhone Duo‘s aspect ratio. When you’re at the Apple Store, check out how your most-used apps look and feel on both the inner and outer displays, and make sure you rotate the inner screen to see how apps behave in this orientation, too — that wide screen could be great for watching vertical videos or scrolling through social media.

If some apps, such as Instagram, look a little different or are wonky, it’ll hopefully be just a matter of time until the developers make an update that optimizes the experience for this new design. Keep in mind that you can also have two apps open onscreen at once, making it easier to multitask.

If you want the best camera experience on an iPhone right now, you should be looking at the iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max, but that doesn’t make the Duo a slouch for shooting photos, either.

Yes, the Duo is missing a third camera (telephoto), and if that’s important to you, then you probably shouldn’t even be considering Apple’s foldable. But still, if you’re going to shell out this much money for a new phone, test out those cameras — even if it’s in a controlled environment like an Apple Store.

Another thing to check out before you pull the trigger is your selfie shots with this new phone. There are two main ways to do this: with the phone closed, holding it up in the regular way you’d take a selfie using the outer screen’s 12-megapixel front-facing camera, or with the inner display open and shooting with the twin 48-megapixel rear cameras (the outer screen will show a preview of the shot).

There’s also a front-facing camera underneath the inner display, which is mostly for video calls — and which we suspect would produce the least-impressive shots from the device. Try them all and see what you think of the pics. And since you’re at an Apple Store, make sure you delete them afterward.

The odd but interesting aspect ratio of the front display on the iPhone Duo may be a little awkward for typing, so it’s best to do a typing test when you have one in front of you. While the inner display will provide a roomier and more comfortable typing experience, you probably won’t want to have to open up the Duo every time you want to shoot off a quick text to someone. If you have bigger hands, typing on the front screen could be a bit of a nightmare.

Typing one-handed on the small cover screen should be manageable, but try it out to see if it works for you. Some may find it convenient; others may find it cumbersome.

And when you’re typing on the inner display, try the Duo in both portrait and landscape orientations to see which feels better. You can also choose between a split keyboard and larger keys. It’s thoughtful of Apple to offer options that let you tailor the typing experience to your preferences, but you may find that none of them suit your style.

#3053. Top Wall Street analysts back these 3 stocks for their long-term growth potential

Major indexes remain volatile as investors assess key earnings releases and geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. Investors with a long-term horizon should look beyond the ongoing noise and focus on stocks that are well-positioned to generate strong returns.

In this regard, recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist stocks with robust growth opportunities. These experts conduct an in-depth analysis of all the macro and micro factors affecting a company, focusing on its long-term growth potential.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

CrowdStrike Holdings is a cloud-native cybersecurity provider. The company recently announced an expanded partnership with Schwarz Digits to bring its Falcon platform to European enterprises.

After hosting several European investor meetings with the CrowdStrike CFO, Stifel analyst Adam Borg reiterated a buy rating on CRWD stock and increased his price target to $230 from $220.

The five-star analyst said that the meetings increased his confidence about CrowdStrike being an "important, well-positioned cybersecurity platform vendor that is an AI beneficiary given its expansive portfolio, unique data set, and ability to both secure AI and use AI to improve security."

Among the key takeaways, Borg noted that AI is driving a major shift in cybersecurity demand as it presents software vulnerabilities that can be exploited by less sophisticated hackers with capabilities that were once limited to government-backed hacking groups. This has led to companies making cybersecurity a top priority, driving customer interest in CrowdStrike's new AI Detection & Response solution and its broader security platform.

Borg added that AI-driven demand is expanding CrowdStrike's pipeline and supporting confidence in the company's higher fiscal 2027 net new annual recurring revenue guidance issued last quarter. Overall, Borg believes that CrowdStrike has multiple growth drivers that can help maintain revenue growth in at least the high-teens and drive improved profitability in the years ahead.

Borg ranks No. 651 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 65% of the time, delivering an average return of 15%. See CrowdStrike Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Moving on to AST SpaceMobile, a company building a global cellular broadband network in space. Recently, Piper Sandler analyst Alexander Potter initiated coverage of space-related stocks. While the analyst assigned AST SpaceMobile a buy rating with a price target of $100, he has a neutral stance on rocket builders SpaceX and Rocket Lab due to valuation concerns.

"We prefer ASTS, due to a more palatable valuation, and a clearer path to EBITDA upside," said Potter.

The five-star analyst highlighted that AST SpaceMobile builds satellites that connect directly to smartphones, ensuring network connectivity for users everywhere and enabling applications like video calls, streaming, and gaming. Potter added that ASTS' technology helps Mobile Network Operators, or MNOs, expand coverage and offer add-on services to travelers and users in remote locations.

Potter ranks No. 708 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 48% of the time, delivering an average return of 17.2%. See AST SpaceMobile Technical Analysis on TipRanks.

Finally, let's look at Broadcom, a provider of custom AI chips and networking solutions. Recently, Morgan Stanley analyst Joseph Moore reiterated a buy rating on Broadcom stock with a price target of $502.

The five-star analyst is surprised by the underperformance of AVGO stock so far this year compared to its peers, especially given continued momentum in AI-driven demand. Moore cited concerns that competitor MediaTek could gain market share from Broadcom in Google's tensor processing unit chip business and investor preference for faster-growing AI chip names as reasons for the underperformance.

While Moore acknowledged that MediaTek's role in Google's TPU business is growing, he contends that it is unlikely to disrupt Broadcom's position significantly. He expects Broadcom to continue to be the major TPU supplier, with about 80% market share. Overall, Moore believes that concerns about a decline in AVGO's market share to 50% or its eventual replacement seem premature.

"AVGO should retain majority share, sustain strong AI growth, and remain a core compute winner, close behind NVDA," said Moore.

The analyst explained that his bullish outlook on Broadcom is based on the company's solid advantage in high-bandwidth memory supply, chip packaging capabilities, and large-scale production. Moore also highlighted AVGO's dominance in AI ASIC chips, strong networking business, and new customer wins.

Moore ranks No. 148 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 60% of the time, delivering an average return of 25.5%. See Broadcom Insider Trading Activity on TipRanks.
